puzzles.background: In this seaside suburb, the streets pay tribute to the leaders who shaped Australia's federal history — every road named for a prime minister.
puzzles.reveal: It was Altona — where every street honours an Australian prime minister.

rounds.clue: I led Australia through the darkest days of World War II, and my famous 1942 speech declared that Australia looked to America 'free of any pangs as to our traditional links or kinship with the United Kingdom.' Who am I?
rounds.tidbit: John Curtin was the first Australian prime minister to hold a press conference in his pajamas.
rounds.explainer: John Curtin served as the 14th Prime Minister of Australia from 1941 until his death in 1945. He is widely regarded as one of the country's greatest leaders, steering the nation through the Pacific War and forging the ANZUS alliance. Curtin famously worked as a timber worker and union official before entering politics, and his Labor government introduced landmark social security policies. He died in office just weeks before the war ended, aged 60.

rounds.clue: I was the 'working man's friend' who, as treasurer, introduced the postwar immigration boom and the Snowy Mountains Scheme. My nickname came from a railway engine. Who am I?
rounds.tidbit: Chifley's prized possession was a model railway engine, which he kept in his office at Parliament House.
rounds.explainer: Ben Chifley, the 16th Prime Minister (1945–1949), was a former railway engine driver who earned the nickname 'Chif' and was beloved for his humility. His government nationalized the banking system, created the Australian National University, and launched the mass immigration program that transformed the nation. Chifley famously said, 'We have a great objective — the light on the hill — which we aim to reach by working for the betterment of mankind.' He died in 1951, still serving as Leader of the Opposition.

rounds.clue: I was Australia's first Labor Prime Minister to win a majority in the House of Representatives, but my government collapsed during the Great Depression. Who am I?
rounds.tidbit: Scullin was the first Australian prime minister to have a Roman Catholic background and the first to be born in Victoria's goldfields.
rounds.explainer: James Scullin served as the 9th Prime Minister from 1929 to 1932, leading Labor to a landslide victory just days before the Wall Street Crash. His government faced the Great Depression's devastating unemployment and the infamous 'Lang Labor' split, leading to his defeat. Scullin was also the first prime minister to appoint an Australian-born Governor-General, Sir Isaac Isaacs. He later served as a respected elder statesman until his death in 1953.

rounds.clue: I was Australia's third Prime Minister, but I served only three months — the shortest term in history. I also founded the Australian Labor Party. Who am I?
rounds.tidbit: Watson's birth name was John Christian Tanck, and he was raised in New Zealand before moving to Australia.
rounds.explainer: Chris Watson, Australia's 3rd Prime Minister (1904), was born in Chile to a British father and a Chilean mother, making him the first and only prime minister born outside Australia until 2015. At age 37, he remains the youngest person to hold the office. Watson's brief term ended when his government lost a vote over the Conciliation and Arbitration Bill, but he later helped found the Australian Labor Party. He left politics in 1906 to pursue business interests.

rounds.clue: I promised to defend Australia 'to our last man and our last shilling' in 1914. I was also the only prime minister to serve three separate terms. Who am I?
rounds.tidbit: Fisher's government established the Royal Australian Navy and the first federal capital at Canberra.
rounds.explainer: Andrew Fisher, the 5th Prime Minister, led Australia from 1908–1909, 1910–1913, and 1914–1915 — the only PM to do so. A Scottish-born coal miner, he introduced the national currency, old-age pensions, and the first federal income tax. His famous 1914 election pledge to support Britain in World War I 'to our last man and our last shilling' became a defining moment of Australian history. Fisher resigned in 1915 to become Australia's High Commissioner to London.

puzzles.theme: World War II battles and aircraft
puzzles.background: In this suburb, the streets pay tribute to the key battles and aircraft of World War II, a common theme in post-war housing developments across Australia.
puzzles.reveal: It was Ashburton, where every street commemorates a World War II battle or aircraft.

rounds.clue: The site of the largest seaborne invasion in history, this battle began on June 6, 1944, a day forever known as D-Day.
options: The Battle of the Coral Sea
rounds.tidbit: The Normandy invasion involved over 5,000 ships and 11,000 aircraft, the largest amphibious assault ever undertaken.
rounds.explainer: The Normandy landings, codenamed Operation Overlord, were the Allied invasion of German-occupied France in 1944. Led by General Dwight D. Eisenhower, the operation saw Allied forces land on five beaches: Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno, and Sword. The success of Normandy marked the beginning of the end for Nazi Germany in Western Europe. The battle resulted in over 425,000 Allied and German casualties, but it established a crucial western front.

rounds.clue: This flying boat was nicknamed the 'Cat' and was famous for its long-range patrols, rescuing downed airmen and hunting submarines.
rounds.tidbit: Catalinas were affectionately called 'Black Cats' when painted black for night missions, and they sank over 100,000 tons of enemy shipping.
rounds.explainer: The PBY Catalina was an American flying boat used extensively in World War II for maritime patrol, anti-submarine warfare, and search-and-rescue. It was renowned for its incredible range and durability, earning the nickname 'The Cat'. Catalinas served with the RAAF and were pivotal in the Pacific, including locating the Japanese fleet before the Battle of Midway. They also rescued thousands of downed airmen, making them legendary among aviators.

rounds.clue: This North African port was besieged for 241 days by Axis forces, but its defenders, including Australian troops, held out and earned the nickname 'The Rats of Tobruk'.
rounds.tidbit: The defenders of Tobruk were called 'The Rats of Tobruk' by German propaganda, but they adopted the name as a badge of honor.
rounds.explainer: The Siege of Tobruk was a prolonged confrontation in North Africa from April to December 1941, where Allied forces, notably the Australian 9th Division, held the vital port against the Afrika Korps. Despite being surrounded and outnumbered, the garrison repelled repeated attacks and survived intense bombing. The siege was a significant morale boost for the Allies and a strategic setback for Rommel. The port's defense secured the supply lines for the British Eighth Army.

rounds.clue: This Libyan city was the site of a rapid advance by Allied forces in early 1941, which led to the capture of over 100,000 Italian troops.
rounds.tidbit: The capture of Benghazi was part of Operation Compass, a five-day raid that turned into a full-scale offensive that nearly expelled the Italians from North Africa.
rounds.explainer: The Battle of Benghazi was part of Operation Compass, the first major Allied military operation in the Western Desert Campaign. In February 1941, Australian and British forces captured the city from the Italian Tenth Army, which was already in disarray. The victory led to the capture of over 130,000 Italian prisoners and the destruction of the Italian army in North Africa. However, the arrival of German reinforcements under Rommel soon reversed the situation.

rounds.clue: This Australian-built aircraft was initially a trainer but was used in combat, and its name comes from an Aboriginal word meaning 'challenge'.
rounds.tidbit: The Wirraway was the first combat aircraft designed and built in Australia, and it was the basis for the Boomerang fighter.
rounds.explainer: The CAC Wirraway was a two-seat training and general-purpose aircraft manufactured by the Commonwealth Aircraft Corporation in Australia. It was based on the North American NA-16, but was modified for local conditions. Despite being obsolete as a fighter, Wirraways were used in combat early in the Pacific War, including the famous 'Battle of Buna' where one crew managed to damage a Japanese Zero. The Wirraway also served as the foundation for the Boomerang, Australia's first locally designed fighter.

puzzles.background: In this leafy suburb, the streets were named after celestial wonders—constellations, stars, and even a planet. Each road pays homage to the night sky above.
puzzles.reveal: It was Balwyn North, where the streets are written in the stars.

rounds.clue: I am the hunter, armed with a club and shield, chasing the bull across the heavens. My belt is a trio of stars that guides skywatchers to me.
rounds.tidbit: Orion is one of the most recognizable constellations, and its two brightest stars, Betelgeuse and Rigel, are supergiants that will end their lives in supernova explosions.
rounds.explainer: Orion is a prominent constellation named after a hunter in Greek mythology, often depicted with a club and shield. It is visible worldwide and contains some of the brightest stars in the night sky, including Betelgeuse, a red supergiant, and Rigel, a blue supergiant. The three stars of Orion's Belt are a famous asterism used to locate other stars and constellations. Orion has been a subject of myth and astronomy across many cultures for millennia.

rounds.clue: I am a brilliant blue-white star, once the pole star around 12,000 BCE. My name comes from Arabic for 'falling' or 'swooping'.
rounds.tidbit: Vega was the first star ever photographed, in 1850, and it is the fifth-brightest star in the night sky.
rounds.explainer: Vega is the brightest star in the constellation Lyra and one of the nearest stars to Earth, about 25 light-years away. It was the northern pole star around 12,000 BCE and will be again around 13,727 CE due to the Earth's axial precession. Vega was the first star to have its spectrum recorded and was also the first to be photographed, making it a cornerstone of astronomical study. Its rapid rotation gives it a flattened shape, and it is about twice as massive as the Sun.

rounds.clue: I am the 'little goat' in the sky, the sixth-brightest star, and I actually form a system of four stars. My name means 'she-goat' in Latin.
rounds.tidbit: Capella is a quadruple star system, with two large giant stars orbiting each other and a pair of smaller red dwarfs farther out.
rounds.explainer: Capella is the brightest star in the constellation Auriga, the charioteer, and is often called the 'Goat Star' due to its Latin name. It is a quadruple star system, consisting of two binary pairs: a pair of giant stars (Capella Aa and Ab) and a pair of red dwarfs (Capella H and L). The main pair are both yellow giants, each about 2.5 times the mass of the Sun, and they orbit each other every 104 days. Capella is relatively close to Earth, about 42 light-years away, making it a popular target for amateur astronomers.

rounds.clue: I am a celestial bull, and my face is marked by a V-shape of stars called the Hyades. My shoulder holds the fiery red star Aldebaran.
rounds.tidbit: Taurus contains the Crab Nebula, the remnant of a supernova observed by Chinese astronomers in 1054 CE.
rounds.explainer: Taurus is a zodiac constellation representing a bull, often associated with Zeus in Greek mythology, who disguised himself as a bull to abduct Europa. It is one of the oldest recognized constellations, with roots in ancient Babylonian astronomy. Taurus contains two prominent star clusters: the Hyades, which form the bull's face, and the Pleiades, located on its shoulder. The star Aldebaran, a red giant, marks the bull's eye, and the constellation is also home to the Crab Nebula, a supernova remnant.

rounds.clue: I am the great bear, circling the northern pole forever. My tail is long and my body is vast, but I never dip below the horizon.
rounds.tidbit: Ursa Major contains the Big Dipper, an asterism that has been used for navigation for centuries, pointing to Polaris, the North Star.
rounds.explainer: Ursa Major, the Great Bear, is one of the most famous constellations in the northern sky, known for its asterism, the Big Dipper. In Greek mythology, it represents Callisto, a nymph turned into a bear by Zeus's wife Hera. The constellation is circumpolar for many northern latitudes, meaning it never sets. The Big Dipper's 'pointer stars' are used to find Polaris, the North Star, making it a crucial navigational tool for travelers and sailors.

puzzles.background: In this suburban estate, the streets pay tribute to the great wordsmiths of the English language. Each thoroughfare is a nod to a literary legend.
puzzles.reveal: It was Bentleigh — where every street is a poet's tribute.

rounds.clue: I wrote of orphans, ghosts, and the harsh realities of Victorian England. My characters include a miser and a young boy who asks for more.
rounds.tidbit: Dickens coined or popularized words like 'boredom' and 'butterfingers' through his novels.
rounds.explainer: Charles Dickens (1812–1870) was the most famous novelist of the Victorian era, known for works like 'Oliver Twist', 'A Christmas Carol', and 'Great Expectations'. His serialized writing style made literature accessible to the masses, and his social commentary highlighted the plight of the poor. Dickens' influence extends beyond literature; his descriptions of London shaped the city's image in the public imagination.

rounds.clue: An Australian writer, I captured the spirit of the bush and the struggles of the common folk. My stories often featured swagmen and drovers.
rounds.tidbit: Henry Lawson was the first Australian writer to be given a state funeral, in 1922.
rounds.explainer: Henry Lawson (1867–1922) was a prolific Australian writer and poet, often regarded as the country's greatest short story writer. His works, such as 'The Drover's Wife' and 'While the Billy Boils', depicted the harsh realities of bush life with realism and empathy. Lawson's writing helped define the Australian national identity, and he is celebrated for his portrayal of mateship and resilience. Despite personal struggles, he left an enduring legacy in Australian literature.

rounds.clue: I wrote an epic poem about the fall of man, and my name is synonymous with grand, majestic verse. My blindness did not hinder my imagination.
rounds.tidbit: John Milton's 'Paradise Lost' is considered one of the greatest epic poems in English literature.
rounds.explainer: John Milton (1608–1674) was an English poet and intellectual, best known for his epic 'Paradise Lost', which explores the biblical story of the fall of man. He was also a civil servant and wrote pamphlets advocating for freedom of the press and divorce. Milton's use of blank verse and complex characters, such as Satan, has influenced countless writers. His work reflects the political and religious turmoil of 17th-century England.

rounds.clue: A Scottish poet, I celebrated the ordinary and the rustic, and my birthday is a national day of remembrance. My most famous work begins, 'O my Luve's like a red, red rose'.
rounds.tidbit: Robert Burns is the most famous poet to have a street named after him in Bentleigh — and his birthday is celebrated worldwide on January 25th.
rounds.explainer: Robert Burns (1759–1796) was a Scottish poet and lyricist, widely regarded as the national poet of Scotland. He wrote in both Scots and English, capturing the essence of rural life and human emotion. His poems and songs, such as 'Auld Lang Syne' and 'Tam o' Shanter', are beloved worldwide. Burns's influence extends to literature, music, and even the celebration of Burns Night, where his works are recited and enjoyed.

rounds.clue: An Irish poet and playwright, I was a leading figure of the Celtic Revival and won a Nobel Prize. My work often reflected Irish mythology and the supernatural.
rounds.tidbit: W. B. Yeats was the first Irishman to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1923.
rounds.explainer: William Butler Yeats (1865–1939) was an Irish poet and one of the foremost figures of 20th-century literature. His poetry drew on Irish folklore, mysticism, and the political turmoil of his time. Yeats co-founded the Abbey Theatre and served as a senator in the Irish Free State. His works, such as 'The Second Coming' and 'Sailing to Byzantium', are celebrated for their profound imagery and philosophical depth.

puzzles.background: In this suburb, the streets pay tribute to the leaders who shaped Australia's federation and its early political landscape.
puzzles.reveal: It was Bentleigh East — where the streets are named for Australian prime ministers.

rounds.clue: I steered my nation through its darkest hours, saying, 'We are in this war to the finish.' My name is synonymous with wartime resolve.
rounds.tidbit: John Curtin was the only Australian prime minister to die in office, passing away in 1945 just weeks before World War II ended.
rounds.explainer: John Curtin served as Australia's 14th Prime Minister from 1941 to 1945, leading the country through the Pacific War. He famously declared that Australia would look to America for its security, not Britain, a pivotal shift in foreign policy. Under his leadership, Australia's forces were brought home from the Middle East to defend against Japan. His wartime leadership made him one of the most revered figures in Australian history.

rounds.clue: I was the architect of Australian federation and served three times as prime minister. My face adorns a coin, but my legacy is a nation united.
rounds.tidbit: Alfred Deakin was known as 'the silver-tongued orator' for his powerful speeches that helped convince Australians to vote for federation.
rounds.explainer: Alfred Deakin was a key figure in the movement that led to the federation of Australia in 1901, and he served as Prime Minister three times between 1903 and 1910. He was instrumental in establishing national institutions like the High Court and the Australian Capital Territory. Deakin was also a strong advocate for a 'White Australia' policy, a complex part of his legacy. After his death, he was honored on the $50 note, and later on the $1 coin.

rounds.clue: I was known as 'the Little Digger' and led my country through the Great War. I once said, 'I am not a party man; I am an Australian.'
rounds.tidbit: Billy Hughes was a fierce advocate for Australia's interests at the Versailles Peace Conference, where he argued passionately for war reparations.
rounds.explainer: Billy Hughes served as Australia's 7th Prime Minister from 1915 to 1923, leading the nation through World War I. He was a fiery and controversial figure, known for his forceful personality and sharp wit. Hughes famously split the Labor Party over conscription, then formed a new government with his political opponents. He remains one of the longest-serving members of parliament in Australian history, sitting for over 50 years.

rounds.clue: I was the first prime minister to be born in Tasmania, and I led a government that took Australia out of the Depression. My nickname was 'Honest Joe'.
rounds.tidbit: Joseph Lyons was the only prime minister to have been premier of a state (Tasmania) before entering federal politics.
rounds.explainer: Joseph Lyons served as Australia's 10th Prime Minister from 1932 to 1939, after leaving the Labor Party to lead the conservative United Australia Party. His government focused on economic recovery and national unity during the Great Depression. Lyons was known for his approachable and honest demeanor, which earned him the nickname 'Honest Joe'. He died in office in 1939, becoming the second prime minister to do so.

rounds.clue: I was a three-time prime minister and the man who promised Australians they would 'fight to the last man and the last shilling' in support of Britain.
rounds.tidbit: Andrew Fisher was a Scottish-born miner who became a key figure in the Australian labor movement and later prime minister.
rounds.explainer: Andrew Fisher served as Australia's 5th Prime Minister on three separate occasions between 1908 and 1915. He was a founding member of the Australian Labor Party and a champion of workers' rights. Fisher's government introduced significant social reforms, including old-age pensions and maternity allowances. His famous 'last man and last shilling' pledge in 1914 was a defining moment of Australian wartime loyalty.

puzzles.background: In this suburb, the streets are named after the native flora of Australia, with each road paying homage to the unique plants and trees that define the landscape.
puzzles.reveal: It was Blackburn, where every street is a tribute to native Australian flora.

rounds.clue: This striking red flower is the state emblem of New South Wales and shares its name with a rugby team from Sydney.
rounds.tidbit: The Waratah is so iconic that it appears on the New South Wales state coat of arms.
rounds.explainer: The Waratah is a genus of five species of large shrubs or small trees native to the southeastern parts of Australia. Its name comes from the Eora Aboriginal people, and it was first described by botanist James Edward Smith in 1793. The vibrant crimson flowers are a symbol of resilience and beauty, often used in floral art. The Waratah is also the official floral emblem of New South Wales, celebrated in festivals and even on the state's flag.

rounds.clue: Named after a naturalist who sailed with Captain Cook, this plant's flower spikes look like bottlebrushes and are a favorite of honeyeaters.
rounds.tidbit: Banksias produce woody cones that can remain on the plant for years, protecting seeds until fire triggers their release.
rounds.explainer: Banksias are a genus of around 170 species in the Proteaceae family, named after Sir Joseph Banks, the naturalist on James Cook's Endeavour voyage. They are known for their distinctive, often large, flower spikes that are rich in nectar and attract birds and insects. These plants are adapted to fire-prone environments, with some species requiring heat to release their seeds. Banksias are a vital part of the Australian ecosystem, and their unique appearance has made them a popular subject in art and photography.

rounds.clue: Known as wattle in Australia, this plant's golden blossoms are a national symbol, and its image appears on the country's coat of arms.
rounds.tidbit: Australia's national floral emblem is the golden wattle (Acacia pycnantha), celebrated on Wattle Day each September.
rounds.explainer: Acacia, commonly known as wattle, is a large genus of shrubs and trees in the pea family, with over 1,000 species in Australia alone. They are fast-growing and thrive in a variety of habitats, from coastal areas to arid regions. The golden wattle (Acacia pycnantha) is the official floral emblem of Australia, and its green and gold colors are associated with the nation. Acacias are also important for their timber, gum, and as a food source for indigenous peoples.

rounds.clue: This plant is also called 'paperbark' because of its peeling, paper-like bark, and its oil is a famous antiseptic.
rounds.tidbit: Tea tree oil, derived from Melaleuca alternifolia, has been used for centuries by Aboriginal people for its healing properties.
rounds.explainer: Melaleuca is a genus of around 290 species, commonly known as paperbarks, honey myrtles, or tea trees. They are found across Australia, often in wetland areas, and are recognized by their spongy, paper-like bark. The most famous species, Melaleuca alternifolia, produces tea tree oil, a powerful antiseptic and essential oil used in cosmetics and medicine. These trees are also important in landscaping and for stabilizing soil in wet areas.

rounds.clue: This tree is the primary food source for koalas and is known for its aromatic leaves, which are used in cough drops and oils.
rounds.tidbit: There are over 700 species of eucalyptus, and they are found almost exclusively in Australia, making it the country's most iconic tree.
rounds.explainer: Eucalyptus, commonly known as gum trees, is a diverse genus of over 700 species, almost all native to Australia. They are among the tallest trees in the world, with the mountain ash (Eucalyptus regnans) reaching heights of over 100 meters. Their leaves contain aromatic oils that are used in medicine, particularly in cough lozenges and decongestants. Eucalyptus forests provide habitat for wildlife, including koalas, which feed almost exclusively on the leaves. They have also been planted worldwide for timber, pulp, and as windbreaks.

puzzles.background: In this leafy suburb, the streets pay homage to the native flora of Australia, with names evoking the scents and colors of the bush.
puzzles.reveal: It was Boronia — where every street is named after a native plant.

rounds.clue: I am a genus of over 360 species, often called spider flowers, and my nectar is a favorite of honeyeaters.
rounds.tidbit: Grevilleas are named after Charles Francis Greville, a founding member of the Royal Horticultural Society.
rounds.explainer: Grevillea is a diverse genus of evergreen shrubs and trees native to Australia and nearby islands. They are known for their intricate, often showy flowers that attract birds and insects. The genus was named in honor of Charles Francis Greville, a notable 18th-century British antiquarian and collector. Grevilleas are popular in horticulture for their hardiness and vibrant blooms.

rounds.clue: My name comes from the Malay word for 'cassowary', because my drooping branchlets resemble the bird's feathers.
rounds.tidbit: Casuarinas are also called she-oaks, but they are not true oaks; they are related to beeches.
rounds.explainer: Casuarina is a genus of trees and shrubs native to Australia, Southeast Asia, and the Pacific. They have distinctive jointed, needle-like branchlets that perform photosynthesis. The name is derived from the Malay word 'kasuari', referring to the cassowary, because the branchlets resemble the bird's plumage. These hardy trees are often used for windbreaks and erosion control.

rounds.clue: My golden blossoms are the inspiration for Australia's national floral emblem, and my name appears in the title of a famous children's book.
rounds.tidbit: The golden wattle (Acacia pycnantha) was formally proclaimed Australia's national floral emblem in 1988.
rounds.explainer: Wattle is the common name for the Acacia genus, which includes over 1,000 species, most native to Australia. The plants are known for their fluffy, golden or cream flower clusters, which are actually composed of many tiny individual flowers. The golden wattle's green and gold colors are also featured on Australia's national coat of arms. Acacias play a vital role in Australian ecosystems, fixing nitrogen in the soil.

rounds.clue: My name means 'sweet-smelling' in Greek, and I am a genus of fragrant shrubs, though this road is named after the suburb itself.
rounds.tidbit: The brown boronia (Boronia megastigma) is highly prized for its intense, sweet fragrance used in perfumery.
rounds.explainer: Boronia is a genus of around 160 species of shrubs in the citrus family, native to Australia. They are renowned for their aromatic leaves and bell-shaped flowers, which range from brown to pink and purple. The name is derived from Greek 'boros' meaning 'sweet-smelling'. Many species are cultivated for their essential oils, particularly the brown boronia, which is used in high-end perfumes.

rounds.clue: My name is the same as the suburb and a fragrant shrub, but this street is a shopping arcade, not a botanical lane.
rounds.tidbit: Boronia flowers are so fragrant that they are often used in potpourri and to scent teas.
rounds.explainer: This street shares its name with the boronia shrub, a quintessentially Australian plant. Boronias are small, woody shrubs that thrive in the understory of eucalypt forests. Their flowers are not only beautiful but also emit a powerful, pleasant scent, making them a favorite in gardens and the perfume industry. The species Boronia megastigma is particularly famous for its dark, fragrant blooms.

puzzles.background: In a western suburb of Melbourne, a post-war housing estate was built with streets named after aircraft and aviation pioneers. Each street here commemorates the machines and people of flight.
puzzles.reveal: It was Braybrook — where every street soars with aviation history.

rounds.clue: I am a Queensland-born aviator who made the first solo flight from England to Australia in 1928. My name is also a famous Australian aircraft company.
rounds.tidbit: Hinkler flew a tiny Avro Avian from England to Australia in just 15 days, a record at the time.
rounds.explainer: Bert Hinkler was a pioneering Australian aviator who set numerous long-distance flying records. Born in Bundaberg, Queensland, he was a test pilot for Sopwith and Avro during World War I. His 1928 solo flight from England to Australia captured the world's imagination. He tragically died in 1933 while attempting to break his own England-to-Australia record.

rounds.clue: I am the aviator who led the first trans-Pacific flight from the USA to Australia in 1928. My nickname was 'Smithy'.
rounds.tidbit: Kingsford Smith's Southern Cross was a Fokker F.VIIb/3m, now preserved at Brisbane Airport.
rounds.explainer: Sir Charles Kingsford Smith was one of Australia's most celebrated aviators. He completed the first trans-Pacific flight in 1928, flying from Oakland, California to Brisbane, Australia. He also made the first non-stop crossing of the Australian mainland and the first flight from Australia to New Zealand. He disappeared in 1935 over the Indian Ocean, leaving a legacy as a national hero.

rounds.clue: I am a two-seat trainer and general-purpose aircraft built by the Commonwealth Aircraft Corporation during World War II. My name comes from an Aboriginal word meaning 'challenge'.
rounds.tidbit: The Wirraway was the first all-metal aircraft designed and built in Australia.
rounds.explainer: The CAC Wirraway was a pivotal aircraft in Australian aviation history, produced from 1939 to 1946. It served as a trainer, army cooperation, and even a makeshift fighter during the Pacific War. Over 750 were built, making it the most numerous aircraft ever produced in Australia. Its design was based on the North American NA-16, but it was heavily modified for Australian conditions.

rounds.clue: I am a piston-engine trainer used by the Royal Australian Air Force in the 1950s and 1960s. My name is an Aboriginal word for 'young eagle'.
rounds.tidbit: The Winjeel was the last piston-engine trainer to serve with the RAAF, replaced by jets in the 1970s.
rounds.explainer: The CAC Winjeel was a basic trainer designed for the Royal Australian Air Force, entering service in 1955. It was known for its ruggedness and forgiving flight characteristics, ideal for training new pilots. The Winjeel remained in service until 1975, when it was replaced by the PAC CT/4. Its name, meaning 'young eagle', perfectly suited its role in nurturing fledgling aviators.

rounds.clue: I am a heavy bomber that served in the Pacific during WWII. My name starts with 'B-24' and I was known for my long range and high speed.
rounds.tidbit: The B-24 was the most produced American military aircraft of WWII, with over 18,000 built.
rounds.explainer: The Consolidated B-24 Liberator was a four-engine heavy bomber used extensively by Allied forces during World War II. It was renowned for its range, speed, and payload capacity, making it ideal for long-range missions in the Pacific. Australian squadrons flew Liberators against Japanese targets, contributing significantly to the war effort. Despite being overshadowed by the B-17, the Liberator played a crucial role in achieving air superiority.

puzzles.background: In this northern suburb, the streets form a literary hall of fame, each one named after a celebrated poet or writer from across the centuries.
puzzles.reveal: It was Bundoora — where every street pays homage to the giants of literature.

rounds.clue: I am the Bard of Avon, the greatest playwright in the English language, whose works include 'Hamlet' and 'Romeo and Juliet'.
rounds.tidbit: Shakespeare introduced over 1,700 words to the English language, including 'bedazzled' and 'lonely'.
rounds.explainer: William Shakespeare (1564–1616) was an English playwright, poet, and actor, widely regarded as the greatest writer in the English language. His 39 plays and 154 sonnets have been translated into every major language and performed more often than those of any other playwright. Shakespeare's works explore timeless themes of love, power, jealousy, and ambition, and his influence on literature and theater is immeasurable. He wrote during the Elizabethan and Jacobean eras, a golden age of English drama.

rounds.clue: I wrote the epic poem 'Paradise Lost', telling the story of the Fall of Man. I was also a civil servant for the Commonwealth.
rounds.tidbit: Milton was blind for the last two decades of his life and dictated 'Paradise Lost' to his daughters.
rounds.explainer: John Milton (1608–1674) was an English poet and intellectual, best known for his epic poem 'Paradise Lost' (1667), which explores the biblical story of Adam and Eve's expulsion from the Garden of Eden. He was a staunch advocate for freedom of speech and served as Latin Secretary under Oliver Cromwell during the English Commonwealth. Milton's works, including 'Paradise Regained' and 'Samson Agonistes', are celebrated for their grandeur and complexity. His poetry profoundly influenced later writers, from the Romantics to modern poets.

rounds.clue: I wrote 'Ode to a Nightingale' and 'Ode on a Grecian Urn', and I believed that 'Beauty is truth, truth beauty'.
rounds.tidbit: Keats trained as a surgeon before dedicating his life to poetry, and he died of tuberculosis at age 25.
rounds.explainer: John Keats (1795–1821) was a leading figure of the second generation of Romantic poets, along with Lord Byron and Percy Bysshe Shelley. Despite his short life, he produced some of the most beloved poems in English literature, including his odes and the narrative poem 'The Eve of St. Agnes'. Keats's work is characterized by rich imagery, sensual language, and a deep appreciation for beauty and mortality. His letters and poems have inspired countless artists, and he is now considered one of the greatest poets of the Romantic era.

rounds.clue: I wandered lonely as a cloud and wrote 'I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud', also known as 'Daffodils'.
rounds.tidbit: Wordsworth served as Britain's Poet Laureate from 1843 until his death in 1850.
rounds.explainer: William Wordsworth (1770–1850) was a major English Romantic poet who, with Samuel Taylor Coleridge, helped launch the Romantic Age in English literature with the 1798 publication of 'Lyrical Ballads'. His poetry celebrated nature, the human spirit, and the ordinary, often drawing on his childhood in the Lake District. Wordsworth's most famous works include 'The Prelude', 'Lines Composed a Few Miles above Tintern Abbey', and 'Daffodils'. He was a key figure in the Romantic movement, emphasizing emotion and individualism over reason and classical form.

rounds.clue: I took the road less traveled by, and that has made all the difference. I wrote about New England life and nature.
rounds.tidbit: Frost is the only poet to have received four Pulitzer Prizes for Poetry.
rounds.explainer: Robert Frost (1874–1963) was an American poet, renowned for his realistic depictions of rural life and his command of American colloquial speech. His works, such as 'The Road Not Taken', 'Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening', and 'Mending Wall', explore themes of nature, isolation, and human choices. Frost's poetry often reflects the landscapes of New England, where he lived for many years. He became one of the most celebrated poets in the United States, reading his poem 'The Gift Outright' at President John F. Kennedy's inauguration in 1961.

puzzles.background: This northern suburb's streets honour the leaders of a young nation, with every avenue and court bearing the name of an Australian prime minister.
puzzles.reveal: It was Bundoora — where every street is named after an Australian prime minister.

rounds.clue: I was the longest-serving prime minister, leading twice across two decades, and my name graces a university, a think tank, and a library.
rounds.tidbit: Menzies once famously declared, 'I did but see her passing by, and yet I love her till I die,' in a speech about the British monarchy.
rounds.explainer: Robert Menzies served as Australia's 12th and 22nd Prime Minister, with a record tenure of over 18 years in office. A founder of the Liberal Party, he presided over the post-war boom and expanded immigration. His 'Forgotten People' speech in 1942 championed the middle class, and he was a staunch monarchist who knighted himself in 1963. He also helped establish the Australian National University.

rounds.clue: I led Australia through the darkest days of World War II, and my wartime leadership is often ranked as the nation's greatest.
rounds.tidbit: Curtin was the first Australian PM to declare that Australia looked to America for its security, famously saying, 'without any inhibitions of any kind.'
rounds.explainer: John Curtin was the 14th Prime Minister, serving from 1941 until his death in 1945. He took office just weeks before the fall of Singapore and rallied the nation against the Japanese advance. Curtin's 'look to America' speech shifted Australia's alliances, and he introduced conscription for overseas service. He died in office from a heart attack, worn out by the war effort.

rounds.clue: I vanished while swimming at a beach in 1967, becoming one of Australia's greatest unsolved mysteries.
rounds.tidbit: Holt was an avid swimmer and had a pool built at The Lodge, but his disappearance at Cheviot Beach remains unexplained.
rounds.explainer: Harold Holt served as the 17th Prime Minister from 1966 until his presumed drowning in December 1967. He expanded Australia's involvement in the Vietnam War and continued the alliance with the US. His disappearance sparked conspiracy theories ranging from a CIA hit to a Chinese submarine pickup. He was the first PM to be born in the 20th century and was known for his charisma and love of surfing.

rounds.clue: I was the 'Little Digger', a fiery orator who led the nation during World War I and the Treaty of Versailles.
rounds.tidbit: Hughes was the only Australian PM to serve for two different political parties — Labor and Nationalist.
rounds.explainer: Billy Hughes was the 7th Prime Minister, serving from 1915 to 1923. He was a fierce advocate for conscription and Australia's interests at the Paris Peace Conference. Known for his pugnacious style, he was nicknamed 'the Little Digger' for his connection with troops. He switched parties after a split over conscription and later helped found the Country Party. He remains one of the most colourful figures in Australian politics.

rounds.clue: I was the first to hold the office, leading the federation of colonies into a new nation in 1901.
rounds.tidbit: Barton resigned as PM to become one of the first three justices of the High Court of Australia.
rounds.explainer: Edmund Barton was Australia's first Prime Minister, serving from 1901 to 1903. He was a key figure in the federation movement and led the inaugural government. Barton's achievements included establishing the High Court and implementing the White Australia Policy. He left politics to serve on the High Court, where he worked until his death in 1920.

puzzles.background: In this leafy eastern suburb, the streets pay homage to the great wordsmiths of English literature, from Romantic poets to Victorian novelists.
puzzles.reveal: It was Burwood — where every street is a verse from the canon.

rounds.clue: I held the pen that wrote 'Theirs not to reason why, theirs but to do and die.' I was Queen Victoria's poet laureate.
rounds.tidbit: Tennyson kept a pet hawk and wore a cloak, and his epic 'Idylls of the King' was a favorite of Queen Victoria.
rounds.explainer: Alfred, Lord Tennyson (1809–1892) was the British Poet Laureate for 42 years, the longest tenure of any laureate. His poems like 'The Charge of the Light Brigade' and 'In Memoriam A.H.H.' captured Victorian sentiment and doubt. He was elevated to the peerage in 1884, the first poet to be made a baron for his poetry alone. His work remains a cornerstone of English literature, with lines like 'Tis better to have loved and lost than never to have loved at all.'

rounds.namesake: The Brontë sisters (Charlotte, Emily, and Anne)
rounds.clue: Three sisters from a Yorkshire parsonage, we wrote novels that shocked and stirred the Victorian age. Our names grace the moors and this street.
options: The Brontë sisters (Charlotte, Emily, and Anne)
rounds.tidbit: The Brontë sisters published their first poems under the male pseudonyms Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell to avoid prejudice against female authors.
rounds.explainer: Charlotte, Emily, and Anne Brontë were 19th-century novelists and poets from Haworth, England. Their masterpieces include 'Jane Eyre', 'Wuthering Heights', and 'The Tenant of Wildfell Hall', which broke new ground with their intense emotional depth and social critique. The sisters' lives were tragically short, all dying before age 40, yet their literary legacy endures. Their father Patrick was a clergyman, and the family's isolated life on the Yorkshire moors heavily influenced their writing.

rounds.clue: I wrote 'Ivanhoe' and 'Rob Roy', and my historical novels made me a baronet. My name is synonymous with the romantic image of Scotland.
rounds.tidbit: Scott's novel 'Waverley' was so popular that his later works were published as 'by the Author of Waverley', and the term 'Waverley novels' was coined.
rounds.explainer: Sir Walter Scott (1771–1832) was a Scottish historical novelist, poet, and playwright who essentially invented the modern historical novel. His works like 'Ivanhoe' and 'Rob Roy' brought Scottish history and culture to a global audience. He was a key figure in the Romantic movement and helped popularize the kilt and tartan as symbols of Scottish identity. Despite going bankrupt in his later years, he wrote feverishly to pay off his debts, a feat that earned him enduring admiration.

rounds.clue: I coined 'the pen is mightier than the sword' in my play 'Richelieu'. My last name begins with a double letter.
rounds.tidbit: Bulwer-Lytton also wrote the opening line 'It was a dark and stormy night' in his novel 'Paul Clifford', which inspired a famous bad-writing contest.
rounds.explainer: Edward Bulwer-Lytton (1803–1873) was an English novelist, poet, and politician. He was a prolific writer of bestsellers like 'The Last Days of Pompeii' and 'Pelham', and his phrase 'the pen is mightier than the sword' from his play 'Richelieu' has become a timeless proverb. He served as a Member of Parliament and was created Baron Lytton in 1866. His literary style was flamboyant, and his legacy includes the annual Bulwer-Lytton Fiction Contest for the worst opening sentence.

rounds.clue: My surname is linked to a famous Australian poet, but this close is named after a local family, not a literary giant. Guess who?
rounds.tidbit: The Pescott family were early settlers in the area, and the close is a rare non-literary street among the poetic names.
rounds.explainer: Unlike the other streets in this suburb, which follow the literary theme, Pescott Close honors a local family who owned land in the district in the early 20th century. The name appears on maps from the 1920s, and the family were prominent orchardists in the region. This exception adds a personal touch to the poetic grid, reminding residents of the area's rural past. It's a reminder that not all street names have grand origins; some simply commemorate the people who lived there.

puzzles.background: In this suburb, the streets bloom with the names of Australia's native flora, from golden wattles to fiery waratahs.
puzzles.reveal: It was Burwood — where every street is a native plant.

rounds.clue: I am the floral emblem of New South Wales, a crimson bloom that bursts from the bush each spring.
rounds.tidbit: The waratah's name comes from the Eora Aboriginal word 'warada', meaning 'beautiful'.
rounds.explainer: The waratah (Telopea speciosissima) is a striking Australian wildflower, known for its large, crimson flower heads that can contain up to 250 individual flowers. It grows naturally in the sandstone country of New South Wales, and its dramatic appearance made it a popular motif in art and design. In 1962, it was officially proclaimed the floral emblem of New South Wales. The plant is also notable for its resilience, regenerating from underground lignotubers after bushfires.

rounds.clue: Named for a botanist who sailed with Captain Cook, my toothy flower heads are a favorite of honeyeaters.
rounds.tidbit: There are over 170 species of banksia, and their iconic flower spikes can be as long as a human hand.
rounds.explainer: Banksias are a genus of Australian shrubs and trees named after Sir Joseph Banks, the naturalist who accompanied Captain Cook on the Endeavour voyage. They produce distinctive, cylindrical flower spikes that are rich in nectar, attracting birds, bees, and small mammals. Banksias are also known for their tough, serrated leaves and woody seed cones that open after fire. They are an integral part of the Australian bush, with many species found nowhere else on Earth.

rounds.clue: My golden blossoms are the national flower of Australia, and my name comes from the Greek for 'pointed'.
rounds.tidbit: Australia's national colors, green and gold, were inspired by the wattle's leaves and flowers.
rounds.explainer: Acacia, commonly known as wattle, is a large genus of shrubs and trees, with over 1,000 species in Australia alone. The name derives from the Greek 'akis', meaning a point, referring to the thorns of some species. The golden wattle (Acacia pycnantha) was proclaimed Australia's national floral emblem in 1988. Wattles are incredibly hardy, thriving in poor soils and dry conditions, and their bright yellow blossoms have become a symbol of Australian identity and renewal.

rounds.clue: My leaves are brewed for a medicinal oil, and my papery bark was used by Aboriginal people for bandages.
rounds.tidbit: Tea tree oil is so potent that it is used in everything from antiseptics to cosmetics.
rounds.explainer: Tea tree (Melaleuca alternifolia) is a small tree native to the northeast coast of New South Wales. Its leaves were used by Aboriginal peoples for centuries to treat wounds and infections, and Captain James Cook brewed a tea from them, giving the tree its common name. The oil extracted from the leaves is now a popular natural remedy with powerful antibacterial and antifungal properties. Tea tree oil is produced commercially in Australia and exported worldwide.

rounds.clue: My flowers are a burst of gold, and my name is often used as a symbol of Aussie mateship.
rounds.tidbit: Wattle Day, celebrated on September 1st, has been a national day of recognition since 1988.
rounds.explainer: Wattle is the common name for many species of Acacia, and it is perhaps the most beloved of Australian native plants. Its fluffy, golden flower heads appear in late winter and spring, signaling the end of the cold season. The wattle has been a symbol of Australian identity since the 19th century, appearing on the Australian coat of arms. Wattle Day, first celebrated in 1910, is now a time to wear a sprig of wattle and celebrate Australian heritage.

puzzles.background: In this leafy suburb, the streets pay homage to the great poets of the English language.
puzzles.reveal: It was Canterbury—where every street is a verse from the masters of poetry.

rounds.clue: I am the poet who 'awoke one morning and found myself famous' after the publication of 'Childe Harold's Pilgrimage.' Who am I?
rounds.tidbit: Lord Byron kept a pet bear while at Cambridge, as college rules forbade dogs.
rounds.explainer: George Gordon Byron, 6th Baron Byron, was a leading figure of the Romantic movement. His works, including 'Don Juan' and 'Childe Harold's Pilgrimage', were celebrated for their passion and rebellion. His life was as dramatic as his poetry, filled with scandalous affairs, political activism, and a heroic death in the Greek War of Independence. Byron's influence extended beyond literature, shaping the very idea of the Romantic hero.

rounds.clue: My 'Ode on a Grecian Urn' concludes with 'Beauty is truth, truth beauty.' Who wrote these lines?
rounds.tidbit: John Keats was a trained surgeon and received his apothecary license in 1816.
rounds.explainer: John Keats, a second-generation Romantic poet, produced some of the most beloved poems in English despite his short life. His work, including 'Ode to a Nightingale' and 'To Autumn', is celebrated for its rich imagery and philosophical depth. Keats trained as a doctor before devoting himself to poetry, and his letters are as acclaimed as his verse. He died of tuberculosis at age 25, leaving behind a legacy that continues to inspire.

rounds.clue: I am the novelist and poet who wrote 'The Lady of the Lake' and 'Ivanhoe'. Which author am I?
rounds.tidbit: Sir Walter Scott's novel 'Waverley' was so popular that his later works were published as 'by the author of Waverley'.
rounds.explainer: Sir Walter Scott was a Scottish historical novelist, poet, and playwright who essentially invented the historical fiction genre. His poems like 'The Lady of the Lake' and novels such as 'Ivanhoe' and 'Rob Roy' captured the imagination of readers across Europe. Scott's work had a profound influence on literature and culture, shaping popular perceptions of Scottish history. He was also a lawyer and a dedicated antiquarian, and his legacy includes the beautiful Abbotsford House in the Scottish Borders.

rounds.clue: I am the author of 'Paradise Lost', an epic poem that retells the biblical story of the Fall of Man. Who am I?
rounds.tidbit: John Milton wrote 'Paradise Lost' entirely while blind, dictating the verses to his daughters.
rounds.explainer: John Milton was a seventeenth-century English poet and polemicist, best known for his epic poem 'Paradise Lost'. His work is renowned for its grandeur, complex theology, and the sympathetic portrayal of Satan. Milton was also a passionate advocate for political and religious freedom, serving as a civil servant under Oliver Cromwell. Despite going blind in his forties, he continued to write, producing some of the most enduring works in English literature.

rounds.clue: I am known as the Father of English Literature and wrote 'The Canterbury Tales'. Who am I?
rounds.tidbit: Chaucer was the first writer to be buried in what is now known as Poets' Corner in Westminster Abbey.
rounds.explainer: Geoffrey Chaucer was a fourteenth-century English author, poet, and philosopher, celebrated for 'The Canterbury Tales'. His work was pivotal in establishing English as a literary language, at a time when Latin and French dominated. Chaucer's tales offer a vivid, often humorous portrait of medieval life, from knights to millers. His influence on English literature is so profound that he is often called the 'Father of English Literature'.

puzzles.background: In the mid-19th century, a wave of patriotic fervor swept the British Empire after the Crimean War. This suburb's streets commemorate the war's key battles, fortresses, and commanders.
puzzles.reveal: It was Caulfield North — where the streets echo the thunder of the Crimean War.

rounds.clue: I lost my right arm at Waterloo, but that didn't stop me from commanding British forces in the Crimea. My name is now a byword for a style of sleeve.
rounds.tidbit: The raglan sleeve, used in military coats and modern fashion, was designed to accommodate his missing arm.
rounds.explainer: FitzRoy Somerset, 1st Baron Raglan, was a British field marshal who lost his arm at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815. He later commanded the British Expeditionary Force during the Crimean War, though he is often criticized for the disastrous Charge of the Light Brigade. Despite his military reputation, his name lives on in the raglan sleeve, a style that extends to the collar, which he popularized after his injury. He died in 1855 during the siege of Sevastopol, reportedly from dysentery and despair over the war's losses.

rounds.clue: A river in the Crimea gave its name to a battle where the British and French defeated the Russians in 1854. What is that river?
rounds.tidbit: The Alma River's name became a popular name for streets, pubs, and even a London hotel after the Allied victory.
rounds.explainer: The Battle of Alma, fought on 20 September 1854, was the first major engagement of the Crimean War. Allied British and French forces, led by Lord Raglan and Marshal Saint-Arnaud, defeated the Russian army under Prince Menshikov. The victory opened the way to Sevastopol and boosted morale at home, leading to the naming of streets and establishments after the battle. The battle is also notable for the first use of the Minié rifle, which gave the Allies a firepower advantage.

rounds.clue: A small port in the Crimea gave its name to a battle famous for a suicidal cavalry charge. What is the place?
rounds.tidbit: The battle is also famous for the 'Thin Red Line'—a British infantry line that held against a Russian cavalry charge.
rounds.explainer: The Battle of Balaclava, fought on 25 October 1854, is remembered for two iconic events: the Thin Red Line and the Charge of the Light Brigade. The latter was a disastrous cavalry charge by British forces, immortalized in Alfred, Lord Tennyson's poem. The battle was part of the siege of Sevastopol and highlighted the military's poor leadership. Balaclava also gave its name to the knitted headwear worn by soldiers to protect against the cold.

rounds.clue: A 'soldiers' battle' fought in a thick fog, where British and French troops fought hand-to-hand against a Russian surprise attack. What was the battle?
rounds.tidbit: The battle was fought in such dense fog that soldiers often could not see the enemy until they were at bayonet point.
rounds.explainer: The Battle of Inkerman, fought on 5 November 1854, was a chaotic and bloody engagement during the Crimean War. Russian forces launched a surprise attack on Allied positions, but the British and French repelled them after intense close-quarters fighting. The battle earned the nickname 'the soldiers' battle' because the fog and terrain made it difficult for commanders to control the troops. It was a costly victory, with heavy casualties on both sides, and further weakened the Russian army.

rounds.clue: A city on the Crimean coast, whose siege lasted nearly a year and ended with its fall to the Allies in 1855. What is the city?
rounds.tidbit: The city's name means 'city of Augustus' in Greek, but it is forever linked to the Crimean War.
rounds.explainer: The Siege of Sevastopol (1854–1855) was the central event of the Crimean War, lasting 349 days. The Allied forces, including British, French, and Sardinian troops, besieged the Russian naval base to cripple Russia's Black Sea fleet. The city's defenses, including the Malakoff redoubt, were fiercely defended, but the French capture of Malakoff led to the city's fall. The siege saw innovations like trench warfare and the use of explosive shells, foreshadowing modern warfare. The Russian defenders eventually sank their own fleet to block the harbor, and the city's fall led to peace negotiations.

puzzles.background: In this leafy suburb, the streets are a tribute to the cosmos, with each thoroughfare named after a celestial body or space concept.
puzzles.reveal: It's Caulfield South — where the streets are written in the stars.

rounds.clue: I am the largest planet in our solar system, with a Great Red Spot that's a storm larger than Earth.
rounds.tidbit: Jupiter's moon Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system, bigger than the planet Mercury.
rounds.explainer: Jupiter, named after the king of the Roman gods, is a gas giant with a mass more than twice that of all other planets combined. Its iconic Great Red Spot is a persistent anticyclonic storm that has been raging for at least 350 years. Jupiter has 95 known moons, including the four large Galilean moons discovered by Galileo in 1610. Its strong magnetic field is 20,000 times stronger than Earth's, creating intense auroras at its poles.

rounds.clue: I am known for my spectacular ring system, made mostly of ice and rock, and I have the lowest density of all planets—I could float in water.
rounds.tidbit: Saturn's rings are about 280,000 kilometers wide, but only about 10 meters thick in places.
rounds.explainer: Saturn, the sixth planet from the Sun, is named after the Roman god of agriculture and wealth. Its rings, composed of countless ice particles, rocky debris, and dust, span hundreds of thousands of kilometers yet are remarkably thin. Saturn is a gas giant with a density lower than water, meaning it would theoretically float in a sufficiently large ocean. Its moon Titan has a thick atmosphere and liquid methane lakes, making it one of the most Earth-like worlds in the solar system.

rounds.clue: I am the hottest planet in our solar system, with a thick, toxic atmosphere of carbon dioxide and clouds of sulfuric acid.
rounds.tidbit: A day on Venus (243 Earth days) is longer than its year (225 Earth days).
rounds.explainer: Venus, named after the Roman goddess of love and beauty, is the second planet from the Sun and often called Earth's 'sister' due to similar size and composition. However, its surface temperature averages 465°C, hot enough to melt lead, due to a runaway greenhouse effect. The planet rotates retrograde, meaning the Sun rises in the west and sets in the east. Venus is the brightest natural object in Earth's night sky after the Moon, often visible as the 'morning star' or 'evening star'.

rounds.clue: I am the 'Red Planet', home to the tallest volcano in the solar system, Olympus Mons, and a canyon system that would stretch across the United States.
rounds.tidbit: Olympus Mons on Mars is nearly three times the height of Mount Everest.
rounds.explainer: Mars, named after the Roman god of war, is the fourth planet from the Sun and the most explored planet beyond Earth. Its reddish appearance comes from iron oxide (rust) on its surface. The planet hosts Olympus Mons, the tallest volcano in the solar system at about 21.9 km high, and Valles Marineris, a canyon system over 4,000 km long. Evidence suggests Mars once had liquid water on its surface, and it is the primary target in the search for past or present extraterrestrial life.

rounds.clue: I am the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun, with a surface that experiences extreme temperature swings from -180°C to 430°C.
rounds.tidbit: Mercury's surface temperatures vary by more than 600°C, the greatest range of any planet in the solar system.
rounds.explainer: Mercury, named after the swift Roman messenger god, is the smallest planet in our solar system and orbits the Sun in just 88 Earth days. Despite being closest to the Sun, it is not the hottest—that title goes to Venus. Mercury has a heavily cratered surface, resembling our Moon, and a large iron core that makes up about 85% of its radius. The planet has virtually no atmosphere, so it cannot retain heat, leading to dramatic temperature extremes between day and night.

puzzles.background: In this northern suburb, the streets pay homage to the art and science of capturing light. Every road is named after a camera, a photographic process, or an optical concept.
puzzles.reveal: It was Coburg North — where every street is a snapshot of photography history.

rounds.clue: I am the eye of the camera, bending light to create a sharp image. My name comes from the Latin word for 'lentil' because of my shape.
rounds.tidbit: The first camera lens was a simple pinhole, but by the 19th century, glass lenses like the Petzval portrait lens could capture images in seconds instead of hours.
rounds.explainer: A camera lens is an optical lens that focuses light onto the film or sensor. The name derives from the Latin 'lens' meaning 'lentil' due to the shape. Lenses have evolved from simple single elements to complex multi-element designs that correct aberrations. The invention of the zoom lens in the 20th century revolutionized photography, allowing photographers to change focal lengths without switching lenses.

rounds.clue: I control the amount of light entering the camera, like the iris of an eye. My size is measured in f-stops, and a smaller number means a wider opening.
rounds.tidbit: The word 'aperture' comes from the Latin 'apertura', meaning 'an opening'. A wide aperture (like f/1.8) creates a shallow depth of field, blurring the background.
rounds.explainer: The aperture is an opening in the lens that controls the amount of light reaching the sensor. It works in conjunction with shutter speed to determine exposure. Aperture also affects depth of field: a larger opening (smaller f-number) produces a softer background, ideal for portraits. Modern cameras use an iris diaphragm with multiple blades to create smooth, circular openings.

rounds.clue: I am the sharpness of an image, the point where light rays converge. In photography, I can be manual or automatic, and getting me right is crucial for a clear shot.
rounds.tidbit: The first autofocus camera, the Konica C35 AF, debuted in 1977, using a simple passive system that measured contrast to achieve sharpness.
rounds.explainer: Focus refers to the point where light rays from a subject converge to form a sharp image. In early photography, focusing was done by adjusting the bellows on large-format cameras. The development of autofocus systems in the late 20th century made photography accessible to everyone. Today, advanced cameras use phase-detection or contrast-detection methods to achieve focus in milliseconds.

rounds.clue: I am an informal photograph, often taken quickly without careful composition. The term originated from a hunter's quick shot, but now I capture everyday moments.
rounds.tidbit: The term 'snapshot' was first used in photography in the 1860s by astronomer John Herschel, who borrowed it from hunting slang for a quick, hasty shot.
rounds.explainer: A snapshot is a photograph taken quickly, often without artistic intent, to capture a moment. The word was coined by Sir John Herschel in 1860, originally referring to a rapid firearm shot. With the advent of affordable cameras like the Kodak Brownie in 1900, snapshots became a popular way for ordinary people to document their lives. Today, smartphone photography has made snapshots the most common form of photography worldwide.

rounds.clue: I am the tiniest unit of a digital image, a tiny square of color. My name is a portmanteau of 'picture' and 'element'.
rounds.tidbit: The first digital image was created in 1957 by Russell Kirsch, who scanned a photo of his son at 176x176 pixels — about 0.03 megapixels.
rounds.explainer: A pixel is the smallest controllable element of a digital image, representing a single color. The term was coined in 1965 by Frederick Billingsley at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Digital cameras capture millions of pixels, and their number (measured in megapixels) determines resolution. The first digital camera, invented by Steven Sasson at Kodak in 1975, produced a 0.01-megapixel image that took 23 seconds to capture.

puzzles.background: In this working-class neighborhood, the street names tell a story of ambition and aspiration—each one borrowed from the halls of English academia. From ancient universities to famed public schools, the streets here are a tribute to the pursuit of knowledge.
puzzles.reveal: It was Collingwood—where the streets are named after elite English schools and universities.

rounds.clue: This university's alumni include Isaac Newton, Charles Darwin, and Stephen Hawking. Its motto is 'Hinc lucem et pocula sacra'—'From here, light and sacred draughts.'
rounds.tidbit: Cambridge's King's College Chapel took over 70 years to build, from 1446 to 1515, and is considered one of the finest examples of Perpendicular Gothic architecture.
rounds.explainer: The University of Cambridge, founded in 1209, is one of the oldest and most prestigious universities in the world. It was established by scholars fleeing Oxford after a dispute with locals. The university is organized into 31 autonomous colleges, each with its own history and traditions. Its alumni include 121 Nobel laureates, more than any other institution.

rounds.clue: This institution's alumni include J.R.R. Tolkien, Oscar Wilde, and 27 British Prime Ministers. Its library, the Bodleian, has been in continuous use since 1602.
rounds.tidbit: Oxford's oldest college, University College, was founded in 1249, but teaching at Oxford dates back to 1096.
rounds.explainer: The University of Oxford is the oldest university in the English-speaking world, with teaching dating back to 1096. It is made up of 39 colleges and six permanent private halls. The Bodleian Library, its main research library, holds over 13 million printed items, making it one of the largest in the UK. Oxford is also home to the famous Oxford English Dictionary, first published in 1884.

rounds.clue: This institution, founded in 1096, is older than the Aztec Empire and the Magna Carta. Its students are known as 'Oxonians'.
rounds.tidbit: Oxford's Christ Church College has a dining hall that inspired the Great Hall in the Harry Potter films.
rounds.explainer: The University of Oxford's exact founding date is unknown, but teaching began in 1096, making it over 900 years old. It grew rapidly after 1167 when Henry II banned English students from attending the University of Paris. The university's colleges are independent, self-governing institutions, and the university itself acts as a federation. Oxford has produced 26 Nobel laureates, 7 poets laureate, and countless world leaders.

rounds.clue: This is the oldest university in the English-speaking world, and its motto is 'Dominus Illuminatio Mea'—'The Lord is my light.'
rounds.tidbit: Oxford's Ashmolean Museum, opened in 1683, is the oldest public museum in the UK.
rounds.explainer: The University of Oxford's motto, 'Dominus Illuminatio Mea', is taken from Psalm 27:1. The university's coat of arms features an open book with three crowns, symbolizing learning and royalty. Oxford is a collegiate system, meaning students belong to both the university and a specific college. The university's influence extends globally, with the Rhodes Scholarship bringing international students to Oxford since 1903.

rounds.clue: This school, founded in 1749, is one of the 'Clarendon Schools' and has educated 19 British Prime Ministers. Its alumni include Winston Churchill and Jawaharlal Nehru.
rounds.tidbit: Harrow's school song, 'Forty Years On', is sung at the end of every term and has been since 1872.

Its historic streets and village-like atmosphere contrast with the bustling city below, making it a unique blend of nature and culture.

puzzles.background: In this suburban estate, the streets are named after the native plants and trees that once covered the land. Each street pays homage to a different species of Australian flora.

rounds.clue: I am the floral emblem of New South Wales, a brilliant crimson bloom that paints the bush in spring. What am I?
rounds.tidbit: The waratah is so iconic that it was featured on the Australian 50-cent coin in 1995.
rounds.explainer: The waratah (Telopea speciosissima) is a striking shrub native to southeastern Australia, known for its large, crimson flower heads. It was first described by botanist James Edward Smith in 1793, who named it Telopea, meaning 'seen from afar' in Greek, due to its visibility in the landscape. The flower is a popular motif in Australian art and design, symbolizing beauty and resilience. Its nectar-rich blossoms attract a variety of birds, including honeyeaters.

rounds.clue: I am the golden bloom that adorns Australia's coat of arms and is celebrated in September. What am I?
rounds.tidbit: Australia's national floral emblem is the golden wattle, a type of acacia, and its colors are the basis for the country's official sporting colors.
rounds.explainer: Acacia is a genus of shrubs and trees, with over 1,000 species found in Australia, known commonly as wattles. The golden wattle (Acacia pycnantha) was formally proclaimed the national floral emblem in 1988. Acacias are notable for their fluffy, ball-shaped flowers, which are actually clusters of many tiny stamens. They are also famous for their phyllodes—flattened leaf stems that serve as leaves—an adaptation to dry conditions.

rounds.clue: I am a genus of trees and shrubs with papery bark, often found near wetlands, and my name means 'black and white' in Greek. What am I?
rounds.tidbit: The tea tree oil used in cosmetics and medicine comes from a species of Melaleuca, Melaleuca alternifolia.
rounds.explainer: Melaleuca is a genus of around 300 species, endemic to Australia, characterized by their fluffy, bottlebrush-like flowers and peeling, papery bark. The name comes from the Greek words 'melas' (black) and 'leukos' (white), referring to the dark trunks and white branches of some species. They thrive in swampy areas and are fire-resistant, with some species resprouting after bushfires. The famous tea tree oil is derived from the leaves of Melaleuca alternifolia, used for its antiseptic properties.

rounds.clue: I am a tree with a swollen trunk that stores water, and my seeds are roasted and eaten by Indigenous Australians. What am I?
rounds.tidbit: The kurrajong's fibrous bark was used by Aboriginal peoples to make fishing nets and baskets.
rounds.explainer: The kurrajong (Brachychiton populneus) is a drought-tolerant tree native to Australia, easily recognized by its glossy green leaves and swollen, water-storing trunk. It belongs to the family Malvaceae and produces bell-shaped flowers that attract birds. The seeds are rich in nutrients and were a traditional food source for Indigenous Australians, who also used the bark for making string and nets. The tree is also valued as a shade tree in parks and streets.

rounds.clue: I am a fragrant shrub with pink or brown bell-shaped flowers, and my name comes from an Italian botanist. What am I?
rounds.tidbit: The brown boronia is so fragrant that it is commercially harvested for its essential oil used in perfumes.
rounds.explainer: Boronia is a genus of about 160 species of shrubs in the citrus family, native to Australia. They are known for their aromatic leaves and delicate, star-shaped flowers, which range from pink to brown. The genus was named after the Italian botanist Francesco Borone, who died in 1794. Many species are popular garden plants, but some are endangered in the wild. The brown boronia (Boronia megastigma) is particularly prized for its sweet scent and is used in the perfume industry.

puzzles.background: In the postwar years, a housing estate rose near a major airport, with every street name ending in 'ana' to honor the aviation company that built homes for its workers.
puzzles.reveal: It was Glenroy — where every street pays tribute to the pioneering Australian National Airways.

rounds.clue: This airline's name echoed the national carrier of a young nation down under, but its initials spelled out a different kind of 'ANA'.
rounds.tidbit: ANA's first flight, in 1936, was a De Havilland Express from Melbourne to Sydney, carrying just four passengers.
rounds.explainer: Australian National Airways (ANA) was founded in 1936 by a merger of several small airlines, and it quickly became Australia's dominant domestic carrier. It was known for its reliable service and innovative safety practices, including the use of flight attendants. ANA's fleet included Douglas DC-3s and later Convair 240s, and it played a crucial role in connecting Australian cities. In 1957, ANA was acquired by Ansett, ending its two-decade run as a major airline.

rounds.clue: I'm a word from the language of the land, meaning 'south' or 'southern wind', and I was the name of a ship that carried passengers across the seas.
rounds.tidbit: The SS Loongana, launched in 1904, was one of the fastest ships on the Bass Strait run, cutting the crossing time to just 14 hours.
rounds.explainer: The SS Loongana was a steel steamship built for the Union Steamship Company, serving the Melbourne-Launceston route. It was renowned for its speed and luxury, with accommodation for over 200 first-class passengers. The ship's name came from an Aboriginal word for 'south', reflecting its southern route. It served for over three decades before being scrapped in 1936.

rounds.clue: I am a place in the outback, a railway siding that became a ghost town, and my name was used for a type of aircraft that flew the mail.
rounds.tidbit: Kadana, in Western Australia, was a lonely siding on the Trans-Australian Railway, and its name was given to a small de Havilland biplane used by ANA's predecessor.
rounds.explainer: Kadana is a remote location in Western Australia, named after a railway siding on the Nullarbor Plain. The name was adopted for a de Havilland DH.84 Dragon, one of the aircraft used by a small airline that later merged into ANA. This aircraft type was a workhorse for early Australian aviation, carrying passengers and mail across vast distances. The Dragon was reliable and versatile, helping to establish regular air services in the 1930s.

rounds.clue: In the language of the Wiradjuri people, I mean 'camp' or 'place of rest', and I was also the name of a famous racehorse that won the Melbourne Cup.
rounds.tidbit: Menana won the 1930 Melbourne Cup, beating the legendary Phar Lap, which was a huge upset at the time.
rounds.explainer: Menana was a New Zealand-bred racehorse that stunned the sporting world by winning the 1930 Melbourne Cup. Phar Lap, the overwhelming favorite, finished third, and Menana's victory was one of the biggest upsets in Cup history. The horse was trained by John Tapp and ridden by Jim O'Sullivan. Menana's name is believed to derive from an Aboriginal word meaning 'camp', and its legacy is still remembered in racing folklore.

rounds.clue: I am a town in Victoria, and my name comes from an Aboriginal word for 'waterhole' or 'pool'. I also share my name with a famous Australian poet who wrote about the bush.
rounds.tidbit: Tarana, Victoria, is a small rural locality, and its name is also associated with the poet Henry Lawson, who wrote a poem titled 'Tarana'.
rounds.explainer: Tarana is a rural area in Victoria, with a name derived from an Aboriginal word meaning 'waterhole'. The town's name was immortalized by the poet Henry Lawson, who wrote a poem called 'Tarana' in the early 20th century. Lawson's poem reflects the Australian bush ethos and the importance of waterholes in the outback. The name was also used for a railway station on the line to the goldfields, adding to its historical significance.

Acacias are known for their fluffy, fragrant blossoms and their ability to thrive in poor soils, fixing nitrogen through their roots. The name 'wattle' comes from early settlers using the flexible branches to build wattle-and-daub huts.
